content: Ethambutol is not recommended for use in children under the age of 5 years due to concerns about the potential development of optic neuritis. This condition can lead to irreversible blindness, particularly in young children who may be unable to report early visual symptoms. However, a review of pharmacokinetic and safety data for ethambutol in children concluded that the risk of ocular toxicity is negligible if the recommended dosages are followed. This is especially true given that ethambutol is typically used only during the intensive phase of tuberculosis (TB) treatment. In the SHINE trial, ethambutol was included in the first two months of treatment, depending on the local policy at the recruitment site, for both the 4-month and 6-month treatment regimens. All children living with HIV in the SHINE trial received ethambutol during the first two months of treatment, regardless of the regimen they were assigned. It is preferred that children living with HIV who are treated with the 4-month regimen receive ethambutol for the first two months of treatment, irrespective of the local prevalence of HIV. Additionally, it is strongly recommended that ethambutol be added to the 4-month regimen for the first two months in settings with a high prevalence of isoniazid resistance or HIV infection. For adolescents aged 12 years and older, weighing at least 40 kg, and diagnosed with pulmonary TB (PTB), a 4-month regimen including rifapentine and moxifloxacin (2HPZM/2HPM) may be considered, regardless of disease severity. However, this regimen should not be used in children under 12 years of age, adolescents with extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) such as TB meningitis (TBM), disseminated TB, osteoarticular TB, or abdominal TB, or in individuals with a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³ or weighing less than 40 kg. It is also contraindicated in pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding women. While baseline drug susceptibility testing (DST) for fluoroquinolones is desirable, it is not mandatory if the patient has been diagnosed using a molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic test (mWRD) that also tests for rifampicin resistance, as fluoroquinolone resistance is rare in drug-susceptible TB cases. This regimen has a high pill burden, higher cost, and limited availability of individual medicines at many treatment sites, which should be discussed with patients and their families. To ensure adequate rifapentine exposure, the regimen should ideally be taken with a modest-fat meal. Daily dosing is recommended throughout the intensive and continuation phases of treatment for all drug-susceptible TB regimens in children. Thrice-weekly dosing is not recommended due to insufficient evidence, and daily dosing remains the preferred approach. Children with peripheral lymph node TB showed no significant difference in unfavorable outcomes between the 16-week and 24-week treatment arms in the SHINE trial. This finding may reassure clinicians about the delayed clinical response often observed in children with peripheral lymph node TB, where lymph nodes may remain enlarged even after treatment, particularly when treated for 4 months. Children and adolescents living with HIV were eligible for the SHINE trial, with 11% enrolled in the 16-week arm and 10% in the 24-week arm. Clinicians may consider treating children and adolescents living with HIV and non-severe TB for 4 months, depending on the degree of immunosuppression, antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, and the presence of other opportunistic infections. Close monitoring is essential, especially at the 4-month mark, with treatment extended to 6 months if progress is insufficient. Children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), defined as a weight-for-height Z-score below -3 or a mid-upper arm circumference below 115 mm, were not analyzed separately in the SHINE trial due to low numbers. As SAM is a danger sign, even children with non-severe TB should preferably receive 6 months of TB treatment. Infants under 3 months of age or weighing less than 3 kg, including those born prematurely, were not included in the SHINE trial. No new data were received on the treatment of congenital TB or TB in very young infants aged 0–3 months. Given the early development of the immune system, infants under 3 months with suspected or confirmed PTB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis should be treated promptly with the 6-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/4HR), as per the 2014 WHO guidance. Dose adjustments may be required to account for age and potential toxicity, and such decisions should be made by clinicians experienced in managing pediatric TB. Children and adolescents treated for TB in the past 2 years were excluded from the SHINE trial due to the increased risk of treatment failure and drug resistance. These individuals should be treated with the standard 6-month regimen (2HRZE/4HR). Children and adolescents with severe pulmonary TB who do not meet the eligibility criteria for the 4-month regimen should be treated with the standard 6-month regimen, which includes ethambutol during the intensive phase (2HRZE/4HR). Children with drug-susceptible EPTB, excluding TBM and osteoarticular TB, should also receive the 6-month regimen. For osteoarticular TB, a 12-month regimen (2HRZE/10HR) is recommended. Children with TBM should be treated with either the 12-month regimen (2HRZE/10HR) or the newly recommended 6-month intensive regimen (6HRZEto). TBM is a severe form of TB that primarily affects young children and accounts for up to 15% of childhood TB cases. It is associated with significant mortality and morbidity, including neurological sequelae, attention deficits, and behavioral disorders. A 6-month intensive treatment regimen has been used in South Africa since 1985 with favorable outcomes, including no relapses in a subset of patients followed for 2 years post-treatment. The short intensive regimen (6HRZEto) has shown lower death rates and higher treatment success rates compared to the standard 12-month regimen but is associated with a higher proportion of neurological sequelae among survivors. Children with TBM should preferably be hospitalized for treatment initiation and close monitoring. Infants under 2 years with miliary TB should be evaluated for TBM, regardless of CNS symptoms. If evaluation is not possible, extending treatment to 12 months may be considered. The short intensive regimen (6HRZEto) is an option for children with bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed drug-susceptible TBM. However, data on its use in children and adolescents living with HIV are limited, and the standard 12-month regimen should be used in this population. In South Africa, children and adolescents living with HIV receive 9 months of HRZEto, but evidence was insufficient for WHO assessment in 2021. The feasibility of introducing the short intensive regimen depends on the setting, with factors such as acceptability, affordability, and access to child-friendly formulations being critical. Ethionamide should not be replaced with ethambutol if unavailable.
